implementation_notes: The metadata store is the decorator set on the class: @Entity("users"), @PrimaryGeneratedColumn(), @Column({ name: "user_name", length: 64 }), @ManyToOne(...); the DataSource reads those decorators (using emitted design-type metadata) into EntityMetadata - columns, relations, indices - and the QueryBuilder/EntityManager engine executes CRUD from it, so no per-entity mapper exists. Because the store is decorators, the build must keep the decorator options and the metadata polyfill in place, or the mapping silently degrades to defaults. TypeORM also documents an EntitySchema object form for teams that want the metadata as data, and Prisma replaces the whole arrangement with a schema DSL plus a generated client.
pitfalls: Decorator-based mapping is a build configuration: changing the TypeScript target or dropping the reflect-metadata import degrades column types without a compile error.
Circular imports between entity files silently drop relations, making the mapping depend on module load order.
Generating the schema from entities (synchronize) is convenient in development and destructive against production data.

variants.name: TypeORM EntitySchema objects (metadata as data)
variants.idiom_name: new EntitySchema({ name, columns, relations, indices })
variants.implementation_notes: TypeORM documents separating entity definition from the class: new EntitySchema({ name: "user", columns: { id: { type: Number, primary: true, generated: true }, name: { type: String } }, relations, checks, indices }) holds the mapping as plain data, optionally typed through an interface (EntitySchema<Category>), and shared columns are composed with the spread operator because schema objects cannot extend a base schema. The same metadata layer consumes it, so a repository built from the schema behaves like the decorated class. Choose it when classes are shared with other layers, when the mapping must be generated or serialized, or when decorators cannot be enabled in the build.
pitfalls: EntitySchema has no inheritance: shared column sets must be spread in by hand and the corresponding interface extended manually.
The link between schema and class is loose, so a name or target that disagrees with the real class fails only when the data source initialises or the repository is used.

variants.name: Prisma schema models with a generated client
variants.idiom_name: Prisma schema model blocks + generated typed client
variants.implementation_notes: Prisma removes the mapping from TypeScript entirely: models, fields, scalar types, keys, relations and the database-side names (@map and @@map) are declared in the schema file, which is the metadata store; the generator reads it and emits the typed client plus the input for migrations, and the client is the engine that executes queries and materialises results. Because the TypeScript types are generated from the same declaration, schema/type drift becomes a build error. Use it when one schema should be the source of truth for both database and client; prefer decorator or EntitySchema mapping when hand-written domain classes must stay the declaration.
pitfalls: The generated client is a build artifact: editing the schema without regenerating leaves the types and the runtime believing the previous mapping.
The schema DSL cannot express every database feature, so raw queries bypass the typed layer and reintroduce hand-mapped rows.
